A B S T R A C T
Low-density steels with di<sup>f</sup>erent aluminium contents have been investigated with an aim to examine the oc-
currence of di<sup>f</sup>erent strengthening mechanisms leading to its higher strength. A composition corresponding to
6.8 wt% aluminium has been studied to understand the underlying strengthening mechanisms. Di<sup>f</sup>erent factors
contributing to the strengthening mechanisms have been separately analyzed. Microstructural features have
been analyzed using Mössbauer spectroscopy, small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), X-ray line pro<sup>fi</sup>le analysis and
transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The enhanced yield strength of the low-density steel containing 6.8 wt
% Al was attributed to the strengthening e<sup>f</sup>ects arising from the ferrite grain size, dislocations incorporated
during processing, ordered phase formation and the presence of Al atoms in the solid solution. Each of these
operating mechanisms was modelled by using its constitutive equation for example, grain size strengthening by
classical Hall-Petch equation and the strengthening from dislocations by Taylor's equation. In addition, the
formation of nano-sized ordered phase was evaluated by TEM, Mössbauer spectroscopy, SAXS and hence order
strengthening was modelled by using the size and volume fraction (as determined by TEM and SAXS).
Strengthening due to lattice frictional stress required for dislocation motion was also incorporated into the
model.

8% [3,4]. These steels, depending on the alloying addition, can form a

4. Discussion
4.1. Analysis of strengthening mechanisms
To get a better insight into the yield strength of Fe-6.8Al alloy fo
the cold rolled and annealed samples, the observed yield strength was
deconstructed into the contribution of di<sup>f</sup>erent strengthening me
chanisms by the application of empirical formulations. The application
of such a procedure in literature has been reported by Kumar et al. [40]
to model the strength contribution in Al-Mg-Sc alloy, by Hajy Akbary
et al. [41] in Fe-3.5Mn-2.9Si-0.3 C steel and Takaki et al. [42] for a Fe-
18Ni-0.001 C steel. In the present study <sup>fi</sup>ve strengthening mechanisms
from (i) dislocations, (ii) grain size, (iii) ordered phase, (iv) solid so-
lution and (v) lattice frictional stress have been used to examine the
yield strength of Fe-6.8Al low-density steel in di<sup>f</sup>erent conditions.
Kumar et al. [40] also used the same strengthening mechanisms to
correlate the yield strength of Al-Mg-Sc alloy to the various micro-
structural parameters such as grain size, dislocation density and pre-
cipitate size.
The strength contribution from solid solution
( \tau _ { \mathrm { s s } } )
has been calcu
lated by the application of equation [43]

\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {\mathrm{ss}} = \frac {\mathrm{G} \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{s}} ^ {3 / 2} \mathrm{c} ^ {1 / 2}}{7 0 0}, \\ \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{s}} = | \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{G}} ^ {\prime} - \beta \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{b}} |, \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{G}} ^ {\prime} = \frac {\varepsilon_ {\mathrm{G}}}{(1 + \frac {1}{2} | \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{G}} |)}, \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{b}} = \frac {1}{a} \frac {d a}{d c} \text {and} \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{G}} = \frac {1}{G} \frac {d G}{d c} \end{array}\tag{9}
where G is the shear modulus, c is concentration of the solute, a is the
lattice parameter,
\varepsilon _ { \mathbf { G } }
is the change in shear modulus per unit change in
concentration of solute and
\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { b } }
is the change in lattice parameter with
change in concentration. By applying the assumptions reported in Ref.
[43] that: the shear modulus increases linearly with composition, the
shear stress required for solid solution strengthening has been derived.
For the above calculations the value of
\mathbf { G }
was taken as 82 GPa, con-
centration (c) was taken as 6.8 wt% and
\varepsilon _ { s }
was taken as 0.45 [43]. The
value of
\tau _ { s s }
was calculated as 95.6 MPa for the Fe-6.8Al alloy. Using the
lattice parameter values measured by XRD in Ref. [15] for Fe-Al alloys,
the solid solution strengthening for Fe-Al alloys has been found to in
crease from 67.8 to 127.2 MPa for the 5 wt% Al to 9 wt% Al respec-
tively. It is to be mentioned here that solid solution strengthening
contribution from Fe-Al matrix is only taken into account while doing
the above calculation by taking the volume fraction of Fe-Al phase. For
very <sup>fi</sup>ne domains, it is di<sup>fi</sup>cult to separate solid solution strengthening
from ordered phase strengthening, hence in such a case the contribution
of solid solution strengthening is ignored.
The lattice frictional stress (τ ) necessary to overcome the intera-
tomic bonding forces during the glide of dislocations on the slip plane
was calculated [44] by equation
\tau_ {\mathrm{PN}} = \frac {2 G}{(1 - \upsilon)} \exp (- \frac {2 \pi a}{b (1 - \upsilon)})\tag{10}
where G is the shear modulus, is the Poisson's ratio, a is the inter
planar spacing and b is the interatomic distance in the slip direction.
For the Fe-Al low-density steels system the value of these constants are

\mathrm { G } = 8 2 \ : \mathrm { G P a } , \mathrm { v } = 0 . 3 3 , \dot { \mathrm { a } } = 2 . 0 2 \ : \mathring { \mathrm { A } } , \mathrm { b } = 2 . 4 8 \ : \mathring { \mathrm { A } } \ : [ 4 3 , 4 5 ]
. By substituting
the values in Eq. (9), we obtain a value of τ ~154.34 MPa. Eq. (10)
provides the lattice frictional stress at 0 K [40]. However, due to the
presence of thermal energy, the stress value required to move disloca-
tions in the lattice at room temperature would be signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly lower
than the value calculated from Eq. (10) [40]. Due to unavailability of
lattice frictional stress data in literature pertaining to Fe-Al alloys, we
have used a value of 41 MPa which has been used by Speich and Swann
[46] for a 0.4 wt% C-steel.

\left( \tau _ { \mathrm { o r d e r } } \right)
can be
calculated by the equation
\tau_ {\mathrm{order}} = 0. 7 \mathrm{G} (\frac {\gamma}{\mathrm{Gb}}) ^ {3 / 2} (\frac {\mathrm{fr}}{\mathrm{b}}) ^ {1 / 2}\tag{11}
where
\gamma

modulus, b is the burgers vector, f and r is the fraction and the radius of
the ordered phase. The determination of the ordered phase size was
done by TEM in Ref. [40] in contrast to both TEM and SAXS based
estimation in our present study.
High angle grain boundaries are known to arrest the motion of

\Delta \sigma_ {\mathrm{GB}} = \mathrm {k_ {HP} D^ {- 1 / 2}}\tag{12}
where D is grain diameter and
\mathbf { k } _ { \mathrm { H P } }
is a constant. The constant
\mathbf { k } _ { \mathrm { H P } }
is
dependent on the composition of the alloy and its microstructural state.

where
\boldsymbol { \rho }

[31] which is applied to (110) XRD peak pro<sup>fi</sup>le as described in Section
2.3. Whereas the dislocation density in Ref. [40] was determined by

4.2. Strengthening from the ordered phase
It is well established that in polycrystalline materials, strengthening
from (i) grain size and (ii) dislocations are the two potential strength

from nano-sized ordered phase can also be considered to be additional
strengthening mechanism operating in the present case. Strengthening
from ordered phase formation can be attributed to the di<sup>f</sup>erence in

pairs thus restricting their mobility and leading to strengthening. In
summary, the splitting of dislocations into super-partial dislocation in
ordered phases leads to increase in <sup>fl</sup>ow stress.

5. Conclusions
The present work reports the observation of enhanced yield strength
in Fe-Al based low-density steels. One of the reasons for the enhanced
strength is due to the formation of nano-sized
\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { A l }
ordered phase
having DO structure, although the major contributions in the overall
strength is due to dislocations and grain size. The characterization of
the ordered phase was done by TEM, SAXS and Mössbauer spectro-
scopic studies. The yield strength of the cold rolled and annealed
samples were then evaluated by the numerical formulation of the
known strengthening mechanisms. Based upon experimental results
and analysis the following conclusions can be drawn.
1. The formation of
\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { A l }
ordered phase has been observed in binary
Fe-Al based low- density steels. These phases have been character-
ized by SAXS, Mössbauer spectroscopy and TEM which shows that
size of the ordered phase to be between 2.5 3.8 nm. The size of the
ordered phase is observed to be increasing with the aluminium
content.
2. The tensile yield strengths of the Fe-6.8Al low-density steel samples
subjected to di<sup>f</sup>erent annealing conditions were modelled with the
available theoretical formulations for various strengthening me-
chanisms. For the cold rolled sample, strengthening contributions
from (i) dislocations (generated during cold rolling) and (ii) grain
size/boundaries were observed to be the dominant. For the fully
recrystallised samples, the contribution to the strengthening me-
chanisms was in the following order: (i) grain size strengthening
(dominant mechanism), followed by nearly equal contribution from
(ii) dislocations and (iii) ordered
\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { A l }
phase. The material annealed
even beyond complete recrystallization underwent higher extent of
ordering, and hence overall strength was due to nearly equal con-
tributions from (i) solid solution strengthening and (ii) order
strengthening.
In summary, it can be stated that the dominance and interplay of
various strengthening mechanisms including order strengthening lead
to the enhanced strengthening in Fe-Al alloys.
